title: Distinct Modes of Quantum Information Transfer in Power-Law Long-Range Spin Networks
authors: E. E. Marshall, C. C. Nelmes, T. J. G. Apollaro, T. P. Spiller, I. D'Amico
abstract: We identify different regimes of quantum state transfer in long-range coupled spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ systems, where naturally occurring power-law interactions enable rapid, high-fidelity transfer with minimal engineering. Across a broad range of interaction profiles, from effectively nearest-neighbour coupling to Coulomb interactions, we show how long-range connectivity fundamentally reshapes the mechanisms underlying information propagation within such systems. For effectively short-range interactions, transfer follows familiar ballistic transfer dynamics: an initially localised excitation spreads across many eigenmodes concentrated within the approximately linear region of the spectrum, enabling robust wavepacket motion. In contrast, increasing long-distance interactions via lowering the power-law exponent $α$ ($α=1-2$) drives a striking transformation, where the initial state becomes confined to progressively fewer eigenmodes, ultimately reducing the dynamics to the coherent participation of only a few states corresponding to the highest eigenenergies. This spectral localization gives rise to emergent long-range oscillations between distant sites, revealing a distinct -- and faster -- transfer mechanism arising from the intrinsic structure of long-range quantum interactions rather than from full-system engineering pathways.
summary: This work analyzes how the range of interactions in a spin chain dictates quantum information transfer dynamics. By varying the power-law decay exponent $\alpha$, the authors distinguish between standard wavepacket spreading and novel, faster transfer modes arising from spectral localization. This has implications for designing robust quantum communication channels.
main_problem: The paper investigates the distinct mechanisms governing quantum state transfer fidelity in spin networks whose interactions decay according to a power law.
main_result: Long-range interactions (low power-law exponent $\alpha$) fundamentally change the transfer dynamics, leading to emergent, faster oscillations confined to a few high-energy eigenmodes, contrasting with the ballistic spread seen in short-range systems.
method: The study uses theoretical analysis of the XX Hamiltonian, calculating quantum state transfer fidelity via single-particle transition amplitudes derived from the system's spectrum.
model_or_system: The model is a spin-1/2 chain governed by an XX Hamiltonian with long-range couplings decaying as $J_{i,j} \propto r_{\alpha}^{i,j}$. The coupling range is controlled by the power-law exponent $\alpha$.
key_observables: Average fidelity $\langle F(t) \rangle$, arrival time $\tau$, and the spectral distribution of the initial state.
important_parameters: The power-law exponent $\alpha$ (controlling interaction range), chain length $N$, and the coupling strength $J_0$.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the transfer of an arbitrary single-qubit quantum state injected at one end of the chain.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of transfer time ($\tau$) on chain length ($N$) and $\alpha$, comparing few-mode oscillations ($\alpha \le 1.5$) to wavepacket propagation ($\alpha \ge 2.0$).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the dynamics across different $\alpha$ regimes, contrasting short-range (ballistic) vs. long-range (few-mode coherent) transfer, and details the optimization methods used to maintain high fidelity.
why_interesting: It provides a theoretical framework for designing quantum channels by tuning interaction decay rates, showing how spectral properties dictate the speed and mechanism of quantum information transport.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Maximal average fidelity as a function of total number of sites N ∈[4, 60] for α-chains, evaluated over a total time window t · J0 = Nπ/2, corresponding to twice the speed limit for perfect state transfer (PST) in nearest-neighbour systems [18]. Horizontal (dashed) line corresponds to the limit in which there is quantum advantage over classical means of communication [51]. In the large-α limit, the XX (effective) nearest-neighbour spin chain is known to lose its quantum advantage for communication at N ≈240 [52].

FIG. 2: A diagram showing an example chain of length N with 4 optimised site positions, with di the distance between two adjacent sites and on-site energies, Bi, on each end of the chain, preserving mirror symmetry.

FIG. 3: Time at which the fidelity is maximal τ plotted as a function of the total number of sites N, across increasing strengths of the power-law exponent α. Inset presents a zoomed-in window of the α = 1 chains, highlighting the distinguishability of the individual data points.

FIG. 4: Top panel shows, for a fixed N = 100 site long-range (α = 2) chain, how increasing the number of optimised boundary sites o, from 0 to 4 leads to near-perfect ( 99.99%) average fidelity and fast transfer time, eventually approaching a saturation regime. Bottom panel illustrates the corresponding optimised spatial profiles of the spacing between sites and local magnetic fields across the lattice: the bulk remains homogeneous with uniform bond strength and zero field modulation, while non-trivial structure develops only near the boundaries.

FIG. 5: Distinct transfer dynamics associated with optimized chains for the selected sequences of α values (left column), alongside the localization of the initial-state distribution in k-space over the ordered spectrum (right column) of the corresponding varied-α, N = 100-site chain.
